title: Mindfulness Seminar 6
speaker: Nomon Tim Burnett
summary: Nomon Tim Burnett takes up the fourth foundation of mindfulness, mindfulness of phenomena or dharmas, in the final week of a six-week seminar on the Buddha's Four Foundations of Mindfulness Sutra. Passing over the sutra's lists of hindrances and factors of enlightenment, Nomon turns to the three marks of impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, and not-self, and offers softness as a way to meet the tension that self-clinging brings. One example is a friendly encounter with an acquaintance while riding the bike home from dropping off Walker at school. Nomon reads from Larry Rosenberg on anatta, closes with Rumi's "The Guest House," and then hears from participants about anger surfacing in practice and the phrase "Life is short, nobody said it was going to be easy, and don't take it personally."

sentences.text: Anyway, remember that the root teaching on mindfulness we're basing all this on is a sutra by the Buddha, the Four Foundations of Mindfulness.
So it's time to talk a little bit about the fourth foundation.
The fourth foundation, probably best translated in English, is mindfulness of phenomena.
In Pali it's mindfulness of dhammas, or you would say dharmas, because they're sort of Sanskrit-centric.
So what do we mean by this?
Mindfulness of phenomena, or mindfulness of dharmas.
"Phenomena" is like a singular noun, and "dharmas" sounds like a plural noun.
We hear the word dharma used in different ways in Buddhism, right?
It's one of the three jewels of Buddhism: Buddha, dharma, and sangha.
It can mean Buddha's teaching; that's what it usually means in the context of the three jewels.
But it also can mean a thought, a sort of irreducible thought moment.

Just like scientists need units, the smallest possible unit they can find, scientists came up with atoms, which at the time they thought were an irreducible unit, but later they figured out atoms are made of smaller things.
There's probably no limit.

But the Buddhist psychologists and the Buddha himself, and all the Buddhas before him if you believe in that kind of stuff, posited that there's a micro moment of reality, the smallest moment you could experience.
That's also called the dharma.
Then dharma also refers to the natural law of the universe.
Like, how do things just go?
That's also the dharma.
So dharma is a moment of reality, the law and flow of reality, and teachings.
That actually does make some kind of sense if the goal of the teachings was to describe reality.
So reality is the teachings about reality and reality itself.

In English, I don't know if they do this in other languages because I don't know if they have that, but in English they usually capitalize the D if it's referring to teachings and lowercase the d if it's referring to an instant of reality.
And so this is mindfulness of all that.
One way to look at it is that the third foundation, which we've been studying the last week, was mindfulness of mind, of citta.
We looked at that last week as the still aspect of mind that's observing the contents.
So the first, most obvious aspect of this fourth foundation is, okay, now we've noticed the contents.
We were noticing the stillness of mind and the relationship between mind and the contents with the third foundation.
And now maybe we're noticing the contents.
The way this section of the sutra is written, the Buddha gives several of his most famous lists, Buddhism being full of lists.
These lists are analyses, ways of grouping the various possible phenomena along different axes.
You've probably heard of almost all of these lists.
One of the lists is the five aggregates, the five skandhas or khandhas, which are mentioned in the Heart Sutra.
One of the lists is the five hindrances, five different varieties of troublesome reality that prevent us from practicing.
Another is the seven factors of enlightenment, which are seven different ways of analyzing reality in helpful, wholesome ways of experiencing the world.
At first when you look at this, it looks like a manual.
Okay.
And when I was first trying to think about what to say about this, I was thinking about it like a manual: okay, so I should tell everybody, avoid these five, really bad.
Do these seven, really good.
And who avoids these five?
Who avoids these seven?
You, right?
You do.
I do.
But then I thought about it a little bit more and I thought, well, that is true in a way, and it would probably be very helpful to do that.
It would probably be good if we actually did memorize some of these darn lists.
Zen students, right?
We're famous for just doing it and just sitting, and we don't really know anything.
So it would probably be good if we knew some of these lists.
Theravadan practitioners memorize these lists and recite them over and over again.
So I think that we should memorize these lists so that we would have some good tools.
These are better tools than our usual tools, is the first layer of meaning, maybe.
Our usual tool is essentially, how do I get what I want, right?
And how do I avoid what I don't want?
And maybe these will be more helpful tools.
But then what I was noticing is that I wanted to speak about those two contrasting lists.
There's a few others in there, but I'll skip them for now.
These five bad things and seven good things that I want: it seems like an obvious contrast.
And I was finding that I did not want to talk at all about the five aggregates, the five skandhas.
Because what the five skandhas are, and this is over here in the Heart Sutra, about form, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness, is a refutation of the sense of self.
We have a certain habitual way of understanding and organizing phenomena that we perceive, right?
It's possible that there is some sort of external phenomena out there, because we all seem to see fairly similar things.
But we have no way of knowing that.
If you think about it, everything that we know about reality is purely through the senses, right, and the mind.
The five skandhas are listed in this section; actually they're listed first.
I found that I didn't really want to talk about them because I still haven't seen that interesting, it seems like sort of boring.
And then I realized, oh well, that's probably why they're the most important.
Because we naturally approach all these things from our habitual, self-identified, self-formed, self-conceptualizing way.
We know very well that material possessions aren't going to make us happy.
But there's a certain grabbiness that we all have about material possessions, we have to admit, and maybe an even stronger grabbiness around spiritual teachings.
We want these ones and those ones and not these ones.

So then I started thinking, well, maybe more important than talking about any of these lists is to see if we can look a little more directly at the underlying teaching of the three aspects of all of these realities.
One of those three aspects is no self.

The Buddha taught over and over and over and over again that the chief delusion, the grand hallucination of our life, which is the hinge pin for suffering, is this belief we have in a solid, separate, enduring person, our belief in me.
This section of the sutra, mindfulness of dharmas, has lots of different ways of analyzing, looking at dharmas.
But then I thought, well, maybe we should look at dharmas a little more carefully and especially look at this teaching of not self.
So that we don't just sort of turn this into another possession, you know what I mean?
Another thing to do, another thing to fail at, another thing to get pissed off that we're not that good at.
Probably other people are going to be pissed off that we're good at.
Probably other people are good at it.
Those monks are good at it, or whatever.

The other thing that's interesting about this section is that even though I instantly, and maybe you would have done better, but I don't know, I instantly was thinking about it from a completely self-referential point of view.
That's not there.
That's not there.
We assume that; we impute that.
There are simply different ways of describing these moments of reality on a different list, different organizational principles, but nowhere does it say there's a person there or a me there.

So I thought for my talk tonight on this fourth foundation of mindfulness, I actually will try to refrain from even telling you any of the content stuff of the sutra, because this underlying teaching is maybe more important.
And I had this idea about softness, which you might have noticed relates to this, as a way to work on this and explore this.
It really is astonishing how pervasive this concept of a person is.
And you can study this in meditation, and probably you are studying this in meditation.
There's some experience, right, as you study mindfulness of breathing or mindfulness of body.
First there's some sense of some experience, and then very quickly, maybe so quickly you don't even notice it a lot of the time, it's me breathing, right?
It's my body, my feelings.
But what Buddha said is that that is habitual, conditioned, and that actually each of these moments of reality has three important aspects.
Because we don't totally get these experientially and directly, we have a lot of trouble.
Sometimes they're called the three marks of reality, and these are also mentioned in the Heart Sutra, which actually sort of refutes the reality of the three marks, but that's another story.
It also refutes the reality of the five skandhas, but that's just a way of getting even softer about all this.
It's to learn about it, fully understand it, and then realize even these teachings are not real.
Everything here is provisional.
So the three marks of reality are impermanence, unsatisfactoriness, and not-self or non-self.
This doesn't sound very cheerful, actually, but it's quite important in liberating because, for one thing, it seems to actually be reality, so trying to deny the reality of this is problematic.
And for another thing, as we live more in harmony and acceptance and softness with these aspects of reality, the less we need to resist and fight the way things are.
And the more we can just enjoy the ride of being a human being with our particular conditions, and work with that with a little more spaciousness, a little more openness.
Impermanence is great because it's so obvious and irrefutable.
Nobody could put up a good argument against impermanence.
Nobody here could say, "Well, most things are impermanent, but not my car, or not a rock, or not a mountain, or even not the earth itself."
We all know that all these things are impermanent.

But if we look accurately and carefully at our attitudes, and the way that we interact with objects and people and our self and our body, if we really look accurately at the implied attitude, not what we say we think, but the implied attitude in how we interact with things, we see pretty quick that even though we can't argue with impermanence, we basically think impermanence is going to happen later.
Right?
Think about it.
We all agree we're going to get sick, and old age and death and all that, right?
Not now.
And then when we do get a cold, we're angry, right?
Because, "Yeah, yeah, I know I have to get a cold sometime, but not now.
I have things to do today."
So impermanence is so obvious, and yet there's a certain little layer there.
We can notice this little layer of denial and resistance and trying to postpone and push away impermanence.
And so it's just a matter of turning towards it, breathing with it: ah, it's here, all the time.
Then unsatisfactoriness is one possible translation of a difficult Buddhist term, dukkha, sometimes translated as suffering.
But it's kind of uncool to say that all reality is suffering, because that's a little confusing.
The way it's expressed, and all these things are so intertwined it's almost silly to have three different words, right?
It's three different facets of one reality.
So the way it's expressed is that things are not satisfactory in the way that we would wish them to be.
That's an aspect of reality, a fundamental aspect of reality.
Any clinging or trying to hold onto something, or have it be something that's going to give us lasting satisfaction, is doomed to not work out the way we hope.
Which is not to say that there is not a sense of satisfaction, happiness and joy.
There is.

But there's a way, sort of the reverse way in which we interact with impermanence, of trying to codify and cling to or rigidify satisfactory things or satisfactory objects or moments or thoughts or desires or feelings of satisfaction.

There's a way that, even when the most wonderful thing happens to you, I don't know what, the most wonderful thing that's happened to you lately, you get the job, you get into college, you get married, whatever, there's a certain moment when these wonderful things in our life come to be, right?
And there's a sense of jumping for joy, right?
You know what I'm feeling?
Like, "Yes!"
And then the second you are on your way up, you can already feel, right, that you're going to be on your way down really soon.
So that's dukkha.
It's that coloring on that joy.
Like, "Oh!"
And then there's a denial of that, and you try to have a party, but pretty soon everyone goes home, right?
Party's over.
There's nothing exactly wrong with that.
It's just, again, becoming more skillful with that as a fundamental aspect of reality, really radically accepting that there's tears and joy, and there's joy in tears, right?
So I want to mention those two, but I really want to spend a little time on this most troublesome one, which is this not-self.
Not-self is a very little translation of the Pali term, which is, what is it again, anatta?
It just means not-self, anatta, yeah.
But I think that not-self, and Norman has talked about this too, is probably too troublesome for us.
We can't really get our minds around not-self, because I feel like I'm a self, don't you?
What do you think?
Not-self just seems sort of drastic.
Or you could try in some forceful way to create some idea of not-self.
You sometimes see people practicing that way, really trying to bear down in their zazen, squash all thinking and eliminate all sense of personality.
Then they create this cockamamie personality, and it's really hard to be around.
So not-self is a little problematic.
I've tried many times to think about this and say something helpful about it, and to see if something different comes up.
It's very slippery, because from the point of view of a conditioned self that's very solid and very believable, you can't just accept a denial of that reality.
So my new thing now is softness of self.

Can we look at the [unclear: "virtual"] ways that we self-identify and, instead of either going along with the usual self-focused show or trying to deny it, just recognize it as a conditioned, contingent reality, as real as anything else?
Can we approach it with softness and non-clinging?
Just turn towards it and have this self as a tool, as a provisional thing.
We need it to get around in the world.
But whenever it arises and starts to turn the screws towards suffering, and how do you know it's starting to turn the screws?
It's when there's stress, when there's tension.
This happens about a billion times a day.
I'm not talking about being hit with a two-by-four.
I'm talking about those little moments.
This morning I noticed one of these.
If you notice one in the morning, that's good.
About a million have just gone by.
I dropped off Walker at school on the bike and I was riding home again, riding by the house of an acquaintance.
He's one of these acquaintances, you probably have someone like this in your life, that you really wish you were good friends with, but it just never seems to quite work out.

He's so friendly, such a nice person, and you really want to be his buddy and hang out with him all the time, but somehow there's never time, and you don't initiate, he doesn't initiate, and it just seems that in this lifetime this lovely person who could have been your friend is just not going to be your friend.
It's the way it goes, right?

So I'm driving by his house, he pulls out of his driveway and rolls down the window and is saying friendly things to me, and I just noticed this moment of intense suffering, like, oh, what do you mean?
And I realized, well, that's this clinging to self.
It's like wanting me to be something in this moment.

So I tried to bring up this softness and joy, to enjoy that moment as best I could, and not to deny the self-concept, the clinging that was arising and causing suffering in the middle of that little friendly interaction.
Nothing wrong with that.
But I tried to bring up, sorry to keep repeating that word, but it's the best I've got right now, softness.
For another thing, I thought I would remind us again of our little recollections verse, because we have no choice, right?
We chanted this verse earlier in the seminar.
We can't hold on to any of this.
It's impermanent.
It's not satisfying in that way.
There's not a self that can endure or even really exist, because *we're of the nature to decay.
We've not gone beyond decay.
We're of the nature to be diseased.
We've not gone beyond disease.
We're of a nature to die.
We've not gone beyond death.* All this applies both in terms of life span, our whole being, but also in terms of every moment.
In that little interaction with my acquaintance that I wish was a friend, there was decay and disease and death and birth and all of that right there.
So this is happening in every moment.
*All that is mine.* See, that word mine is there very deliberately, right?
*Anything you think that is mine, dear and delightful, will change and vanish.* And then we have this little riff on karma.
*I'm the owner of my karma.
I'm born of my karma.
I'm related to my karma.
I live supported by my karma.
Any karma I will do, wholesome or unwholesome, that I will inherit.* And again, karma just means action.
So that's pretty much my whole central point about this fourth foundation of mindfulness: mindfulness of dharmas, of reality itself.
How does reality actually go?
It has these three aspects, which we're in denial of in some ways, and in some ways not.
Nothing's fixed here, right?
Sometimes we're in various relationships to all of these realities.
Sometimes we are completely contented and at peace with all this.
We have to recognize that too.
We can cheer ourselves up a little bit.
But the thing that's interesting about self-concept in practice is that our usual measurement of how things are going is self-based, right?
How am I doing?
When we're really in harmony with dharma, the self-concept is very quiet, so we might not even notice that we're in harmony with reality.
You know what I mean?
There's not necessarily a me there saying, yay!
I'm in harmony with reality and suffering has stopped.
There might just be an absence of suffering, a sense of calm, not very much of a me or an I even arising.
I think almost all of us have some experiences in meditation where there's a little dropping into something quieter.
Then usually about a millisecond later the self-concept arises and says, oh cool!
How do I keep this going?
And then that's [unclear: "cleaning"], right?
See what I mean?
That's the [unclear: "Nile"] of not-self and it short circuits the whole thing.
But anyway, it's still functioning even though you don't necessarily know it.
So here's my practice suggestion, just to reiterate.
Then I want to read another quote from Larry Rosenberg, because he has his own words for saying this, so maybe his words will be helpful too.

It's to notice, in formal practice and also in daily life, and this is the last time I [unclear: "write"], so this is your permanent homework assignment if you want it, whenever there is some tightness, some tension, and it could arise from any of these different loci that we've been studying in our mindfulness.
Tension in the body, tension in the breath, right?
Some of us had really interesting experiments with tension in the breath.
Tension in the feelings.
Tension around desiring or aversion, liking, disliking.
Tension in emotional life, tension in thinking and planning and all that.
Tension arises from any of these places.
You actually notice, ah, that's tension.
And then you meet that tension with softness, softening maybe in some way around it, like I was saying during the yoga.
Maybe sometimes, you know, sometimes tension is really strong, you know?
Suffering can be very strong.
It can be a compelling thought or an angry thought or a hurt, wounded thought.
But it's so strong, it's so believable, and it just keeps you [unclear: "peeing"], right?
Sometimes you can turn towards that directly and just soften with it.
Sometimes maybe you can soften the whole container.
Let that angry, tense, tight little nugget of pain just be there, but let it exist in a soft universe or an ocean, a warm ocean.
And you can use different language.
Softness is just a concept, right?
There's actually no soft or hard thoughts.
This is just concept.
This is not actually real.
So whatever concept seems helpful: warmth may be helpful, coolness might be helpful, softness might be helpful, breathing just without concept could be helpful.
So, to notice tension from any source.
The mindfulness teachings do talk a lot about noticing causes of things, so it could be helpful to notice where that is arising from.
But maybe then it becomes a big complicated psychological thing, and there's nothing wrong with psychology.
I wanted to mention a few things about psychology, because these teachings of non-self are not too familiar to us.
They are not particularly existent, as far as I understand, in psychology, which has emerged from our western mind, right?
It's not like psychology is some separate science over there.
It just emerged from our collective consciousness.
That psychology is concerned with a healthy self, and that's a wonderful thing to have.
There's nothing wrong with that: taking care of the self, self-esteem.
Psychology is interested in having a healthy self.
So this is not to undermine that, but to recognize the limitations of it, and to let that healthy self just soften into nothingness, just fade out, because ultimately it's not reliable.
A healthy self arises according to conditions, right?
You can have conditions in your life, including hiring John Wiley for a few years, which would be a great idea, to help you create conditions in which the self is healthy and supported.
It's hard to get around without a healthy self.
But these teachings are reminding us that the foundations of that are not strong, that conditions are going to change sooner or later.
Conditions are constantly in flux from moment to moment anyway, and that healthy self is not solid.
It's arising and falling, arising and falling.
And then eventually, all of us are on our deathbeds.
That's when we need something more fundamental, something enabling us to address the nature of reality more directly.
That's why I'm bringing up these teachings on softness.
No self to hold on to.
Maybe that's the way to say it.
It's not that there's no self.
Sure, there's a self.
There's no self that you can hold on to or depend on.
Which is not to say you shouldn't depend on it.
See what I'm saying?
You should depend on yourself, but realize that you can't.
I mean it.
I might be getting myself too far out there, let me think.
We should recognize that we are psychological beings, that all this has a strong reality for us and a huge impact on our ability to function and feel happy and secure.
But we hold that self lightly, because we understand that it's skillful means, that it's a temporary conditioned fabrication.
We should get all the help we need to help weave a nice strong fabrication.
But then also see, well, it's like a hammock, right?
See the holes in it, even as we can rest.
You can rest in a hammock.
Wonderful.
Very relaxing.
A little bad for your back, but very relaxing.
But it has holes in it.
So the self is that way.
Well, let's try Larry Rosenberg.
See how he says this.
He said:
*Students love to hear me talk about rapture and deep states of happiness.
But as soon as I talk about anatta, about no self, all I see is wrinkled brows and disgruntled expressions.
And afterwards I get all kinds of difficult questions.
There's no self, who gets enlightened, who gets enlightened, and so on.
And for a while I shied away from talking about this.
But whether students like it or not, anatta is an essential part of the Buddhist teaching.* He's saying that there's no enduring core to the self.
It has no abiding substance.
*And that is a curious statement to make.
Because our whole life is lived on behalf of notions of self that are constantly in flux.
It's as if we are an employee of the ego and it's a full-time job trying to build it up.
Build up the sense of self.
It wants more money, more possessions, more fame, better sex, a bigger car, a new house, or for another kind of person, better meditation, deeper samadhi, and a major enlightenment experience.
Right now, if possible.
This process of appropriating everything as me or mine is constantly going on and has as its whole basis the existence of a self.
So trying to get something implies there's a self trying to get something.
And that according to the Buddha is a delusion, a very high class of hallucination.
We all have it.
In its most extreme form, it is a spiritual disease.
And it is at the heart of all our suffering.
When asked to sum up all of his teaching, the Buddha replied, to paraphrase slightly, under no circumstances, attached to anything as me or mine.*
Don't attach to something as me or mine.

You can go back to any of the contemplations we've been through, and this is the dark side of practice, and see that in one way or another we were claiming all of these practices as me or mine: my mindfulness, my meditation, my breath, my experiences, and so on.
What this teaching tells us is that because everything that arises passes away, there's a certain stress or suffering as a part of life.
We cause that suffering by trying to hold on to these changing things, by making self out of them.
The things you're identifying as self are merely mind states that you're going through.
They exist, but not in the way you think they do.
They are not self.
We get very caught up in the content of our mind states.
This is really true, isn't it?
We get caught up in the content of our mind states.
People in our culture in particular give this content huge amounts of attention.
They might spend years tracing some mental formation back to its source: why am I thinking this?
But that isn't the object of Buddhist practice.
Taking up the contemplations of mindfulness can bring about a dramatic change in one's perspective, shifting us away from the content.
So not so [unclear: "softer"] about the content.
You can see in a certain sense the content doesn't actually matter because whatever it is passes away anyway.
Every mental formation is equal to every other.
None has an enduring core.
And we tend to dismiss or even resent that perspective.
Do you use that arising in the mind?
Because our thoughts seem important to us, and the concept of impermanence seems abstract, irrelevant, and impractical.
And we definitely think that, like [unclear: "Alice"], it's just idealistic, isn't it?
Is that really practical?
As a skillful teacher, the Buddha allows for our attachment to the thought process.
He allows for our attachment to the thought process, and he gives us mindfulness practices to help us have a look.
But at some point, when we've looked and looked, we've finally had enough.
We have heard the content of our mental formations so many times that we are sick of them.
We're ready to move past mental formations, past the contents of our minds, to a deeper kind of wisdom.
And I think that's definitely an important aspect of it, which we need to just give ourselves to: allowing ourselves to wear ourselves out.
Not to be in a hurry.
This is going to take a while, because we're so used to our habitual thought patterns and self-concept.
It may take 50 years or a few lifetimes to finally say, okay, I guess that wasn't satisfying after all.
And what's the other possibility here?
So again, the idea is not to squash the self, but to turn towards all that arises with some equanimity, with some spaciousness, again with some softness.
Just let it in.
The faith component here is that the heart will naturally align itself with reality.
That's the faith piece of this, which is maybe reinforced over time in practice, or maybe it isn't, and you should do something else.

But it's a little by little seeing that, for all my intelligence and all my ideas and all the things I'm trying to figure out, there's some root element of this, which is just letting go, just letting the heart open to what is without interference, without manipulation, which is a little bit scary.
So then it's working also with all the fear and afflictive emotions that arise underneath that or around that.
Maybe I'll close with the poem by Rumi that I opened with last time.
I didn't tie it in very well, and then it just dropped off the map.
So I want to bring Rumi back into the equation.

This is a wonderful poem about the way in which we're trying to be so selective about what experiences we want to let in, and that there's some way that strong habit is a hindrance, an important hindrance, to merging with reality the way it is and practicing this fourth foundation of mindfulness, mindfulness of reality.
This poem is called The Guest House.
*This being human is a guest house.
Every morning, a new arrival, a joy, a depression, a meanness, some momentary awareness comes as an unexpected visitor.
Welcome and entertain them all.
Even if they are a crowd of sorrows who violently sweep through your house and empty its furniture, still treat each guest honorably.
He may be clearing you out for some new delight.
The dark thought, the shame, the malice.
Meet them at the door laughing and invite them in.
Be grateful for whoever comes, because each has been sent as a guide from beyond.*
*This being human is a guest house.
Every morning, every moment, a new arrival, a joy, depression, a meanness, some momentary awareness comes as an unexpected visitor.
Welcome and entertain them all.
Even if they are a crowd of sorrows who violently sweep your house empty of its furniture, still treat each guest honorably.
He may be clearing you out for some new delight.
